maker.odd: Three of these consoles are made by {value}. Which one isn't?

released.sort: from the first released to the most recent
released.era: Drop each console into the decade it came out.
released.shot: In what year did the {label} come out?

rows.label: PlayStation 3
rows.description: video game console developed Sony Interactive Entertainment
rows.hook: used a sleek black case and struggled with a notoriously hard-to-program processor at launch

rows.label: Xbox Series X and Series S
rows.description: home video game consoles developed by Microsoft
rows.hook: comes in two sizes, one built for full 4K power and a smaller, cheaper digital-only version

rows.label: PlayStation Portable
rows.description: handheld game console by Sony
rows.hook: played movies and music off small proprietary discs alongside its handheld games

rows.label: Nintendo Entertainment System
rows.description: third generation home video game console
rows.hook: revived a crashed home gaming market with a gray box and a gray zapper gun

rows.label: Wii
rows.description: seventh-generation home video game console by Nintendo
rows.hook: got whole families waving a motion-sensing remote around the living room together

rows.label: Nintendo DS
rows.description: Nintendo handheld game console
rows.hook: opened with two screens, one of them touch-sensitive, folded shut like a clamshell

rows.label: Nintendo 3DS
rows.description: portable 3D dual-screen handheld by Nintendo
rows.hook: added a glasses-free 3D effect you could dial up or down with a slider

rows.label: Nintendo GameCube
rows.description: sixth-generation home video game console by Nintendo
rows.hook: played its games off small purple disc cartridges shaped like a cube

rows.label: Nintendo 64
rows.description: fifth-generation home video game console by Nintendo
rows.hook: was one of the last major home systems to stick with cartridges instead of discs

rows.label: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
rows.description: fourth-generation home video game console by Nintendo
rows.hook: introduced a wide, rounded gamepad with shoulder buttons and four differently colored face buttons

rows.label: Game Boy
rows.description: 1989 portable video game console
rows.hook: ran for dozens of hours on a handful of AA batteries with its dim green-tinted screen

rows.label: Sega Genesis
rows.description: fourth-generation home video game console developed by Sega
rows.hook: pitched itself against a rival with a blast-processing marketing slogan and an edgy blue mascot

rows.label: PlayStation Vita
rows.description: portable game console developed by Sony Computer Entertainment
rows.hook: packed a bright OLED touchscreen and two analog sticks into a slim handheld

rows.label: Wii U
rows.description: eighth-generation home video game console by Nintendo
rows.hook: paired a traditional controller with a second screen you could hold like a tablet

rows.label: Atari 2600
rows.description: home video game console by Atari
rows.hook: popularized the plug-in cartridge format for home gaming rooms everywhere

rows.label: Game Boy Color
rows.description: handheld Nintendo video game console introduced in 1998
rows.hook: finally brought a full-spectrum display to a wildly popular black-and-green handheld line

rows.label: TurboGrafx-16
rows.description: fourth-generation home video game console
rows.hook: was marketed as the first sixteen-bit home system, beating bulkier rivals to market

rows.label: Nintendo DSi
rows.description: handheld game console by Nintendo
rows.hook: added two screens and a built-in camera to a handheld line, letting you snap and edit photos on the go

rows.label: Game & Watch series
rows.description: handheld electronic game series developed and published by Nintendo between 1980 and 1991
rows.hook: packed a single built-in activity into a credit-card-sized handheld with a tiny LCD screen

rows.label: Neo Geo
rows.description: cartridge-based arcade system board and home video game console developed by SNK
rows.hook: brought arcade-quality games home, famous for its very expensive cartridges

rows.label: Atari Jaguar
rows.description: Fifth-generation home video game console by Atari
rows.hook: was pitched as the first 64-bit home system but flopped despite the marketing claim
